Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this amendment, I simply want to reiterate the approval that our Party gave to it during the course of the committee hearings. I would remind Members of the House that in the major reform of the Crown Corporations Bill that our Government brought in a year ago, one of the primary objectives was to ensure that there would be parliamentary scrutiny of any sale or disposition of a Crown corporation in order to maintain accountability and a sense of review and assessment about specific proposals made by a Government.
We established that principle on the grounds that this would ensure that Crown corporations were not sold without public interest being properly defended or recognized. Had the original measures in the present Bill been allowed to go through without such an amendment, the Government could essentially short circuit that principle because it would have the right to sell to anyone it chose rather than designating a particular buyer.
When I was the Minister of Transport we had very specifically put forward the idea, as a terms of reference of sale, that it should be sold to native Canadians, particularly in northern Canada. The whole purpose of putting the Northern Transportation Company Limited up for sale was to provide an incentive for economic development and economic self-sufficiency on behalf of native people. That was part of the basic criteria by which any sale would be measured.
If there is no specific enunciation as to who the purchaser would be-as provided in the original Bill-theoretically the vendor, the Government of Canada in this case, would have the right simply to cancel the proposed deal with the two native organizations and sell, as it previously intended, to Northern Industrial Carriers, which had no native participation at all. I am not saying that we mistrust it, but it is very
important in this case to establish the precedent by which we deal with the sale of Crown corporations.
Who knows, some day the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), may get around to selling some of those Crown corporations that he promised to sell six months ago. Therefore, it is a very important principle that any Bill dealing with the sale of a Crown corporation should in fact enunciate and specify who is the purchaser and at least what kind of criteria will be established to determine who the purchaser will be.
I suggest it makes good sense for the Bill to provide for the specifics of who the purchase is limited to, and we strongly endorse the notion that this amendment be adopted at this point in time. We think it would not only make the intention of the Government much more clear-cut and entrenched in the statutes, it would also establish an important precedent for future sales of Crown corporations.

The whole purpose of having Parliament consider a Bill authorizing the sale of a Crown corporation is to provide some certainty as to the conditions of sale, who is buying it and what kind of deal the Government has entered into. An organization is being taken out of the public sector and moved into the private sector. There has to be a rationale, especially when the criteria have been set. In this case it happens to be a preferred sale to native organizations in northern Canada. However, we are equally concerned about the precedent set by this Bill. For example, let us say for the sake of argument that the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) comes in with a Bill to sell off de Havilland or Canadair and says that he will sell it to anybody. They should say that they do not want to have Parliament reviewing it. All we are saying is, simply, that there has to be something to review.

The Minister has indicated that he will sell this corporation to two native organizations. We take that on face value. If that is the case, what is wrong with having it in the legislation? Let us say the Bill is passed today. In that event the Minister could say tomorrow morning: "Oops, I'm sorry, I cannot make a deal with those two organizations. He said: Mr. Speaker, I guess you could call Motion No. 3 a private enterprise type of motion. It would ensure that the present owners, namely the people of Canada, get value for what they own. Fair value is a common business term and I am sure my colleagues in the Conservative and Liberal Parties know that. Lawyers always use the term "reasonable man" and everyone seems to know what that means, and the term "consideration" refers to getting some money or other value in exchange for something. The term "fair value" simply means what it says. We get what it is worth.
I am sure, I am hoping and I am reasonably confident that the Government would want to get fair value and would work at getting that unless it does not believe in fair value for anything that the Crown owns and is selling. Northern Transportation Company selling, fair value is not okay. Surely no one, and particularly no member of the Conservative Party, would believe that.
Since this is the first sale of a Crown corporation requiring legislation in this Parliament, it seems to me that we should not allow this legislation as it is presently worded to be a model for the sale of other Crown corporations or government assets of any other kind. That is the reason I moved the first amendment and Motion No. 3.1 did that because the Bill is so vague that it could serve as a model for the sale of any or all Crown corporations and assets simply by changing the names. Surely we do not want the legislation to be so loose that any Minister could use it. It is not very likely that the Minister of Transport would use it, but I cannot say the same thing about some of the other Ministers. I think that this Bill as it is presently worded sets a bad precedent. That is why I said at the outset that I had very mixed feelings about it. We are going along with it in this specific instance only because the corporation is being sold to people of the North. If it were not, then as a matter of general principle we would be opposing it right down the line and the Government sure as hell would not get the Bill through by the end of this month. Because it is an exceptional case, we are prepared to agree to it. However, if the Government insists on keeping the Bill as vague as it is now, then it will have a problem.
I hope that no one in this House will disagree with the proposition that the taxpayers who are the owners of the corporation should get fair value for what they own. I would hope that this amendment will meet with the approval of the Government. I hope members will not want to get involved in a long series of rabbit trails regarding the definition of fair value. That would be totally unproductive; it would probably be counterproductive. Fair value in the context of what is reasonable is arrived at by agreement and it ends up in an agreement for sale. What is wrong with putting, in the legislation that allows the Minister to proceed with the sale, the definition of fair value for those assets? This agreement is one between the Crown and two native organizations which belong to the private sector, so surely the same principles that apply to the private sector should apply here. Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief on third reading. I just want to say that I am somewhat disappointed. In addition to the mixed feelings that I had at the outset of the debate and second reading on this Bill, I now have to add disappointment because the legislation as presented by the Minister is so general and vague as to provide pretty well a blank cheque for the Minister to do

June 27, 1985
Northern Transportation Company
anything he wants in the disposal of assets owned by the people of Canada.
We attempted in committee and again at report stage to get the Government to accept a very few amendments. We could have moved a lot more, but we held them to a minimum-I think a total of six yesterday, only four today-to try to get the Government to at least put some basic fundamental changes in the legislation because, while I have great respect for the honesty and forthrightness and integrity of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), I do not feel that way about the rest of the Cabinet. This will not be the last occasion in this Parliament when we get legislation for the so-called privatization of assets of Crown corporations on which the taxpayers of Canada have invested billions of dollars, and I doubt if they will get their money back.
The problem we face is that this legislation that we are dealing with now can serve as a model for each subsequent time. I want to say to the Members of the Government right now that as and when that happens they need not look for the kind of co-operation on those occasions that they got from the Opposition on this one. I repeat, Sir, we make an exception to our basic fundamental disagreement with the sale of a Crown asset properly owned by the taxpayers, and particularly when it is a winner and making a profit. The taxpayer, like any other private individual investor, is just as much entitled to an opportunity for a return on that investment as are others in the private sector. The selling off of the winners denies the taxpayer getting back some, if not, all, of the investment he made.
We make the exception in this Bill because it is being sold to the right kind of people. It is being sold to two Inuit organizations in northern Canada. They will have direct say and responsibility not only in the ownership, but in the operations of the Northern Transportation Company Limited and in the provision of adequate and reasonable transportation services in the North.
On behalf of my colleagues, I wish those two Inuit organizations well in their endeavours. I think I can say for all Members that they will have the full support and assistance whenever possible from Members of the House of Commons. We hope the Government will continue to be of assistance, even though it no longer has any ownership in the corporation, in any way it can so that those two organizations can improve upon the operations of the company and even enlarge on the services that are presently being supplied.
The Northern Transportation Company has been and is now an excellent example of what can be done for people in a region of Canada by all the people of Canada. It served as an excellent example of how they are not discriminated against by insufficient or extremely high cost transportation just because of where they happen to live. In the years of start up and development it lost money, but the people of the nation as a whole shared in the costs. If it had had to be paid for only by the people of the North, they would never have started it. That is a good example of where it is perfectly logical to have a publicly-owned Crown corporation in an area that provides an
essential service, meets a public need and serves the national interest.
If it was logical to have all kinds of competition in areas that are an essential public service it would be, I suppose, logical to have competing sewer and water systems, competing highways, competing sidewalks, competing telephone lines-and we are faced with that prospect as well-or competing power lines. If the private enterprise principle was carried to a logical conclusion that is what would be attempted to be done, but if anybody tried to do that they would be locked up, I hope.
There are some areas in our economy where it is proper for the public, through the Crown, to own and operate an essential public service, particularly in areas that are, in practice, natural monopolies. In those sectors of the economy it must be a publicly-owned Crown corporation or it could be a joint ownership of the Crown and the co-operative movement, for example. It could be a joint ownership between the Crown and in this instance, for example, the two Inuit organizations in northern Canada. This is why we suggested at an earlier stage in this debate that we thought it would be good if the Crown kept 10, 15 or 20 per cent interest in the company because then it would be able to provide assistance as and when the need is shown. It would have been able to provide access to the kinds of technological change and whatnot the Government is able to get much easier than a small company. However, the Government chose to sell the complete Company. So be it.
I hope that the Government will keep in mind that it cannot have just a mindless, total opposition as a general principle to having Crown corporations, that there should not be any at all. Decades ago the Government of Canada started getting into public ownership, not because it believed in it but because the private sector either failed or would not or could not provide something that was an essential public need in the national interest. Too often the Crown went into ownership of a private sector corporation not because it was right in principle to have it a Crown corporation owned by the people of Canada, but to bail out the investors who were going to lose, in one classic case the formation of the Canadian National Railways, something in the order of one and one half billion dollars on five bankrupt railroads. Canadian national was formed to make sure that the banks, trust companies and bond holders got their money. That was the main reason, but as well, it was in the national interest to keep the railways going. That is not the case in this instance.
As I said earlier, the only reason we are agreeing to this sale is because it is being sold to the people most directly concerned. I hope that the new owners of Northern Transportation Company Limited will be able to meet, negotiate and enter into agreements with one or more Dene organizations and will be able to join with them in partnership in the ownership and expansion of the company. That would go a long way toward creating more co-operation among the aboriginals in northern Canada.

In closing, I would say that we wish the new owners well when the agreement is signed, sealed and delivered. However,
I would like to tell the government House Leader that the next time this happens, the Government had better word the Bill a little better. If it does not, it is going to have a problem.

Mr. Speaker, I rise primarily to congratulate the Government for having the good sense to follow through on a major initiative of the previous Government. It is always good to see that even as government Members stumble and fumble around in Budget manipulations, they have some modicum of good sense as indicated by the continuation of initiatives that we began.
I am pleased to see that the basic objective we established over a year ago when putting the Northern Transportation Company Limited up for privatization will be followed as it relates to native organizations in the North. Parenthetically, for Tory Members who are again trying to re-write history, when the Clark administration considered this legislation in 1979, no mention was made of ensuring that the Crown corporation would be sold to native people. It was simply to be put on the block. I would ask government Members to read their history books with an eye for accuracy as opposed to an eye for fantasy.
It is important to ask how we go about dealing with the privatization of Crown corporations. It should not be done in the obsessive, ideological way in which the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) pursues things. It should be done because it is clearly in the public interest. Crown corporations were originally established to serve a public purpose. However, conditions have changed. Public purposes have become altered. It is becoming more important to put these public services back in private hands rather than maintaining them in the public sector.
There were two primary reasons for putting NTCL up for sale. One was that any future expansion of the company would require more equity. In order for NTCL to remain a healthy economic organization, it was going to have to diversify into trucking and other forms of commercial enterprises which really did not justify public investment. To maintain public control and ownership of the company would have meant that it would have stagnated.
In order to provide for the continuation of a healthy transportation unit in northern Canada, the company needed to complement its activities with other forms of economic interests. Therefore, to acquire new forms of equity capital, it had to go on the public market. At the same time, though, it seemed to us that this was a unique opportunity for us to sell a viable, operating company to native people who are now trying to establish their own form of economic development and entrepreneurship. That is why when we announced the proposed sale we stated that preference would go to northerners and native organizations.
Last December, we were deeply concerned when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) announced that the original sale arrangement was with a company from southern
Northern Transportation Company Canada which at that time was not involved with native people. We raised several questions about that, and we are glad to see that the decision has been reversed.
The greatest regret I have about this Bill is that it is a lost opportunity. This Government uses the language of privatization with great frequency. It is one of the hallmarks of the new economic regime. Unfortunately, the Government failed at the first opportunity it had to privatize a company in a reasonably effective and proper way. The Government did not seize the opportunity offered by the sale of NTCL to sell a Crown corporation in a fiscally accountable way. The Bill is sloppy and ramshackled. The Government lost the opportunity to establish proper guidelines and precedents for future sales.
All of the questions that we have been raising over the last several months regarding the intentions of the Government when it comes to privatization have not been answered. Here was a great opportunity for the Government to clearly demonstrate how it would deal with Parliament and the public when coming to grips with the sale of Crown corporations. That is a matter of no small import because we know that there are a number of other Crown corporations, some of great magnitude, that are also being offered for sale.
Many times we asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion how they intend to privatize companies and we received no answers. Here was a chance for the Government to put privatization into practical application. However, the Government did everything wrong.
To begin with, the Government totally ignored the board of directors. The board of directors of a Crown corporation has a very important fiduciary relationship with the corporation. Boards of directors are established not simply to provide room for appointments for friends but to provide a very real policymaking role in the running of Crown corporations, yet the Minister of Transport totally evaded any involvement on the part of the board of directors of this Crown corporation. I would suggest that it would be a serious mistake if that practice was followed in future sales.
Second, the Government almost deliberately short circuited what we believed to be a very important step to take before the sale of any Crown corporation, and that was to do a proper financial evaluation and have that evaluation made public so that the Government could put a proper value on what it was selling. Again, the Minister explained that things have been rushed and that there have been renegotiations, but the kind of study that we commissioned last spring has not been brought forward. An Hon. Member said that there was a study made in 1980, but that had nothing to do with it. We commissioned a specific financial evaluation last spring from First Boston, a financial evaluation which has not been produced.
Third, the Government failed on the question of ensuring that there would be proper disclosure and information requirements in the legislation so that when the sale was finalized, there would be a complete accounting before Parliament and the taxpayers. In part, we have been dealing with this Bill under a large haze and the Government has camouflaged what

is really going on. I think it is a credit to the Minister of Transport that we would take his word on these matters. However, I am not sure that that is the proper way to do business. To repeat the words of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), we certainly do not intend to do that when the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion brings something forward because he is a Minister of a very different kind. We think that now is the time for the regulations and procedures to be properly established.
We support the Bill, as it was our initiative in the first place. I am glad to see that it has come to fruition. We are pleased that native organizations in northern Canada will have an opportunity to manage a good company. We believe that it is good for public policy purposes. However, we deeply regret the way in which it has been done. We had a chance to establish a very important guide-post for the future. That has been lost. Maybe it is a symptomatic sign from the Government. Where managing public business is concerned, the Government still has a great deal to learn. We hope that it will learn.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few brief comments regarding the privatization of NTCL. I would like to extend my thanks to the Liberal and NDP members who have been involved in the legislation. For a short time they have set aside their ideological preoccupations and have seen reason. In fact, it was the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) who initiated the process, even though Liberal candidates in the 1980 election ran on the platform of maintaining NTCL as a Crown corporation. That was the Liberal promise of the time. However the Liberals changed their minds, as they often do. This time the change is for the better.
I would like to compliment the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) on the continuing interest which he has shown in the matter. His task is now all but accomplished. There have been many difficulties involved in the process of privatization. It is my hope that those who were involved, and those who are likely to be involved again, will have learned from the mistakes which have been made in the case of NTCL.
I would like to comment briefly on the tendering process. It became apparent during the course of the debate that it had already been established that the majority shareholding of NTCL would be sold to a native corporation. There were other people who placed bids and did a lot of work in compiling their proposals. I have some doubt as to whether those people were given proper consideration. There is absolutely nothing wrong with a formal native organization such as IDC, DDC or others
becoming involved, but the normal type of business firm which is made up of people of all ethnic origins, who are not ethnically restricted, should also have been given a fair deal on the bidding. I suspect that did not happen and that the deal was weighed in favour of one particular type of organization from the beginning. Some of the firms which I know were interested were owned by native people and not collective organizations. If that arrangement could be known beforehand, in the future it could be made public in order that people would not waste their time bidding on something for which they do not stand a chance of being successful.
I look forward to a new regime in the Mackenzie waterways, the Beaufort Sea and the waterways on the Arctic coast. We are moving away from the idea of a Crown corporation monopoly on certain types of services. We are moving toward a competitive system in which each shipping firm will be given the same type of opportunity. They will be awarded water licences by the WTC on the basis of free competition. Hopefully, we will move away from the system of having to obtain licences from the WTC to a deregulated system.
I would like to wish the new owners of NTCL all possible success. I hope their venture will be profitable. I know that my friend from Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) wished them all the best. I imagine it is difficult for him to hope that the enterprise will be profitable. However, on this side of the House we have no hesitation in hoping that the business will prove to be very profitable in private hands. The best way for it to be profitable is to provide good service throughout the entirety of its service area.
I would like to be associated with the remarks of the Hon. Member for Regina West concerning the possibility of extended ownership. I hope the new owners of NTCL will be able to properly manage the corporation. They have embarked upon a risky venture. The health of NTCL is dependent upon the health of the northern oil and gas industry and the decisions which will have a great bearing on that industry. Those decisions are as likely to be made in Abu Dhabi with an association of Arab oil ministers as they are in Canada or elsewhere. The owners have certainly involved themselves in a risky venture. It is not expected that they will ask the Government to bail them out if they are not successful. They have made their bed and they must lie in it. I hope they will be profitable, and that people will be properly serviced. I hope that the taxpayers will not be asked in the future to become involved again in the shipping business.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a pleasure for me today to speak to third reading of Bill C-25. This Bill has been a long time in coming and its passage will mark the beginning of a new era of farm income stabilization in this country.
The Bill was referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture on May 21 where it received a very careful and extensive review. The committee heard from officials and representatives of most provincial Governments, as well as from organizations whose members in some way could be affected by this legislation.
I would like to make a comment at this point. Yesterday during the debate on the report stage of Bill C-25, a number of speeches were made and there were some interesting observations made by a variety of Members. I am not going to dwell on the motions. I will try to keep my remarks consistent and to the point in dealing with the specific issue at hand. However, there were a number of charges made yesterday, some of which were quite off the mark and some of which were quite false.
With respect to one observation, I think the particular language used might lead people to believe there was some manoeuvring or some attempt to ensure that representations made by certain provincial Ministers or by provincial Departments of Agriculture were avoided. During the course of these hearings, myself and members of the committee learned a great deal about the wide scope of interests within the agricultural community. As a result, certain amendments were recommended. I would like to take a few moments now to explain these amendments, all of which I sponsored, so that Members representing all regions of Canada will understand them very clearly.
The first amendment is to Clause 8 which deals with preconditions to entering into agreements. This amendment addresses the very real concern expressed by certain commodity groups and provinces not only about top loading, but about bottom loading and side loading. The Province of Saskatchewan pointed out quite accurately that top loading is not the only issue. The amendment recognizes this concern by allowing the Minister of Agriculture to consider matters other than just top loading during the course of negotiating commodity agreements.
I believe we get distracted and confused when we start dealing with this piece of legislation because normally when the Government brings in a piece of legislation, the law changes tomorrow. Something happens. A new set of laws are imposed on a commodity group, a sector of the economy or of society. Of course, that interpretation is a wrong interpretation. However, it has caused us some concern and confusion. This Bill does change a number of very important things with respect to the way in which the Act will affect people after it receives third reading, but those are changes from which we can all benefit.
This Act does not impose plans on commodity groups at all. There seems to be a lot of misinterpretation of this legislation, particularly in the media and by certain farm leaders and individuals. Understanding that perhaps we are all to blame for that does not change the fact that we have to face the facts. The amendment, as I indicated, recognizes the expressed concern by allowing the Minister of Agriculture to consider matters other than just top loading during the course of negotiating commodity agreements. The Act provides the legal framework to do certain things that we have to do here in Canada, but it does not impose marketing plans. This clause also recognizes that no agreement resulting from negotiations with the provinces and producers should lead to over-production or have the effect of putting any one region in the position of having an advantage over another region.
The second amendment also reflects the fact that the committee listened carefully and responded to the representations of producers and provinces. Members of the committee found themselves constantly reminded that this program is intended for all commodity groups. It appears we were not only sidetracked by the Bill being a permissive Bill, one which simply involved enabling legislation because it does not establish plans and so on. We got side-tracked into thinking it is only a cow-calf program, or only for slaughter cattle or sheep, when
DEBATES__________________ June 27, 1985
in fact the broad framework of this enabling legislation will allow any commodity group to develop tri-party stabilization programs. I should clarify that by saying "any" is accurate enough. It is a safer word than "all" because it would not allow all commodity groups to form plans, most particularly those commodities dealt with under supply-management. Therefore, we do not have a problem there. Even though this particular clause in the Bill was found to be suitable for red meat, it was found to be too restrictive for horticultural products. Therefore, this amendment to Clause 8 provides greater flexibility for the negotiation of horticultural agreements.
The last three amendments all address essentially the same matter, that of monitoring, and they seek to clarify and broaden the term. The Province of Saskatchewan, along with several other groups, brought to our attention the need for amendments aimed at specifying our intentions for monitoring and administration. The point was well taken because the success of these agreements will depend to a considerable degree upon the quality of their administration. In addition, it was suggested that since each agreement will be unique, the administration agreement for each commodity should also be unique. Therefore, like the Bill itself which provides a framework to negotiate tri-party stabilization plans, these amendments will also establish a tri-party approach to administering those plans as well. They will allow the administrative committee the power to administer individual agreements as specified in each negotiated agreement.
Bill C-25 has been the subject of considerable discussion for a long period of time. It has been spoken to in this House and debated by members of the Standing Committee. The discussions began at the grass roots and evolved to the point where we are today. In fact, this legislation is based on a decade of discussion and the amended version before us today is a result of what we learned in committee. We listened and responded to what we heard.
The time has now come to put this long awaited legislation into effect. To me, this Bill means opportunity. It is the opportunity for us to sit down with the provinces and the commodity groups and hammer out made-to-measure tri-party stabilization programs. It is an opportunity for producers of all commodities to become involved in a comprehensive stabilization scheme. It is an opportunity for Canada to resolve some of its trade difficulties by implementing an insurance oriented stabilization scheme which will be viewed favourably by our trading partners. It is an opportunity to reduce inter-provincial rivarly and the confusing market signals given by the complex assortment of stabilization programs now in place. It is an opportunity to make our livestock industry more competitive. It is an opportunity to do just as the Bill's title implies, bring a greater measure of income stability to the farm sector so that the efficient producer prospers.
The last point is especially important because the agri-food industry directly employs 1.4 million Canadians and brings in more than $10 billion a year in export revenue. Last year it generated about $20 billion in cash receipts while retail sales
June 27, 1985

in the agri-food industry are in the neighbourhood of some $60 billion. Producers are heavily dependent on factors beyond their control, both with respect to natural hazards and market conditions. Crop insurance provides protection against hail, drought, floods and other natural hazards. Stabilization programs are farmers' protection against changing market conditions. That is why we have an obligation to offer producers the best stabilization package possible, and I believe Bill C-25 does exactly that.
I have listened carefully to what producers groups and provincial Governments have said about this legislation. As a result, amendments were brought in but I feel compelled to point out, as I have on previous occasions, that this legislation is only the framework for future agreements. Each plan for each commodity group will be put in place only as a result of negotiation with and consent by the federal Government, the provinces and the commodity group concerned. I am reminded of a statement by a spokesperson for the Canadian Cattlemen's Association when he appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture regarding this Bill. He said:
First, we will give our commitment that we will be at the bargaining table tomorrow if this government wants to take on all the programs, bottom and top-loading, or side-loading or underhand-loading or whatever you want to call them. We will be here to work on them.
This statement epitomizes the attitude that will make Bill C-25 work. 1 can guarantee the House that, given the opportunity to negotiate which this Bill provides for, we will go to the bargaining table and work out agreements to suit individual requirements of each province and each commodity group. I urge all Members of the House to give the Government, the provinces, the farm leaders, and the commodity groups across the country the opportunity which is so desperately needed at this point in time.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity to speak on third reading of Bill C-25 which has been before the Committee on Agriculture for several months. It proposes important changes to the stabilization legislation which is available to farmers across the country. The Minister said that this Bill ushers in a new era in agricultural stabilization. That may be true if the legislation is actually utilized.
When this Bill was introduced, at least four groups supported the establishment of a tripartite red meat stabilization program for lamb, beef, and hogs. I am not sure whether any of the producers in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, or Ontario clearly understand what the amendments introduced last Thursday afternoon actually mean.
Yesterday I spoke with a senior representative of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. After examining the clause which prohibits provincial Governments from having stabilization programs and requiring that if they take part in a tripartite stabilization program they would have to phase out their existing provincial programs he said, "Producers are thoroughly confused as to what the amendment means and
Agricultural Stabilization Act
won't support it because they don't know what it means". He said that the Cattlemen's Association and hog boards of all four provinces had the same feeling.
When representatives of those provincial Governments appeared before the committee, they made it very clear that they did not want any substantive changes to the legislation but wanted it passed as it was. They also wanted to ensure that the tripartite red meat stabilization program would be administered jointly by the three parties to any agreement; the federal Government, the provincial Governments, and the producer groups. Everyone is trying to figure out exactly what the amendment introduced by the Minister last Thursday means, but it clearly puts the Minister in the position of judging what level of stabilization is being provided by the various producer groups involved.
My colleagues and the solicitor for the Canadian Cattlemen's Association also concluded that this amendment allows the Minister to judge whether the stabilization provided actually gives additional benefit to those provided by other bi-partite stabilization programs in any of the provinces not participating. They suggest that the benefits from a tri-partite stabilization program must not be greater than those provided to any producers not party to the agreement.
There is a great deal of confusion on the part of those provinces which did not consent to the original agreement and were not party to it. The Minister has not made proposals or recommendations to resolve their concerns. For instance, the four Maritime provinces were requesting a grain transportation program to be coupled with a program for Maritime Canada which would allow them to operate on an equal basis. We have had no commitment from the Minister that he is willing to do that. Therefore, the concerns of the Maritime provinces have not been resolved. As well, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick have requested that potatoes be designated as a named commodity under the legislation. 1 put forward such an amendment in committee but it was voted down. That certainly indicates the support which exists for the Atlantic region.
The confusion which has developed in this area leaves the possibility of a red meat stabilization program unresolved. The amendment moved by the Minister did not meet the requirements of the producers in Quebec. Not only has this Bill created great confusion for the hog and beef producers in the four participating provinces, it has also not met the demands of Atlantic Canada, Quebec, or British Columbia which did not originally take part in the proposed agreement.
The Minister's consideration of the representations made to the committee have not met the requirement to have a national program. It is clear that this is enabling legislation, but there is a great need and demand in the country now for a proper national tripartite red meat stabilization program. That certainly has not been accomplished. That is why I find the Minister's comment that this is a new era in agriculture stabilization rather hollow. I do not think it will be fulfilled.

June 27, 1985

subsubtopic: PLAUT REPORT-METHOD AND TIMING OF CONSULTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) tabled the long-awaited report by Rabbi Plaut on refugee determination. Two long months after the report was handed over to the Government, it was tabled in the House. Was the delay intentional, to prepare the report for a first-class burial, since summer is ideal for that? I certainly hope not.
The Plaut Report was well received in circles concerned with immigration. Rabbi Plaut states that receiving refugee status is not a privilege but a right. That is fundamental, and will, I hope, form the basis for the entire process.
Agencies and lawyers whose concern is immigration are looking forward to the consultation promised by the Minister of Employment and Immigration, so that we can finally have a refugee determination procedure that is fair, humane and efficient. I therefore suggest that the Minister of Employment and Immigration make her announcement on when and how consultation will take place as soon as possible. I sincerely hope that the summer recess will not be used to bury the Plaut Report. Immigration lawyers and agencies expect the Government to do better than that-the ball is now definitely in your court!

Mr. Speaker, the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada is a positive, healthy influence in society. This organization promotes responsible human sexuality through information and education.
I have received 243 letters from informed, concerned citizens including individuals, volunteers, professionals and organizations,. stating their support for the valuable work that the Planned Parenthood Federation does, and their hope that the Government will make it possible through continued funding for this organization to continue to serve Canadians. Many of
these letters, which were addressed in good faith to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), apparently have fallen upon deaf ears. We are four months into the fiscal year and Planned Parenthood has received no indication from the Minister of National Health and Welfare on the status of its funding.
Overhelming numbers of Canadians believe that they have the right to determine the number and spacing of their children. Planned Parenthood organizations throughout Canada believe that information, education, and services should be available to assist individuals to exercise that right in an informed, responsible manner.
Lack of information about funding contradicts the spirit of the 1969 amendment to the Criminal Code which recognized that dissemination of birth control information was a basic human right and guaranteed all Canadians universal access to family planning.
Teenage women are at great risk today.
I regret I must inform the Hon. Member that her time has expired.

subtopic: AIR-INDIA CRASH-DEATH OF DR. YELAVARTHY NAYUDAMMA
AIR-INDIA CRASH-DEATH OF DR. YELAVARTHY NAYUDAMMA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that all Hon. Members share the grief of the many Canadian families who lost loved ones aboard the Air-India flight which crashed while flying from Canada. To all those people we extend our deepest sympathy and, in my case in particular, to the family of Mrs. Barsa Kelly, a friend of mine from Guelph for many years.
Also aboard that flight was a most distinguished citizen of India, Dr. Yelavarthy Nayudamma, a scientist of such towering international reputation that his advice was sought by people from all over the world, including fellow scientists.
Dr. Nayudamma was returning to India from Canada where he had been attending one of the regular meetings of the Board of Governors of the International Development Research Centre. He was one of ten non Canadians, all of the highest scientific rank, who served diligently on the board of this remarkable institution, one which is regarded within developing countries as a superb example of Canada's aid program but which, sadly, is less well known in Canada.
A week ago tonight I had dinner with Dr. Nayudamma. It pains me to know that he is no longer available to the developing world and to Canada.

subtopic: THIRD WORLD FESTIVAL IN DRUMMONDVILLE, QUE.
THIRD WORLD FESTIVAL IN DRUMMONDVILLE, QUE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to invite my fellow MPs and all Canadians to come to the riding of Drummond this summer for the World Festival of Folklore. The festival has something for everyone. There will be folklore groups from everywhere in the world, all keen to show us their traditional way of life through dance, music, and song. Last year the third of these festivals attracted 400,000 people, which gives an idea of how successful is the event.

The World Folklore Festival in Drummondville is being held for the forth time, and this year about half a million people are expected to attend between July 5 and July 15.
Twenty folk dance groups from all over the world, including the United States, France, the Soviet Union and also Canadian participants from Quebec, Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia, will come together for ten days of folk dancing and folklore.
There will be all kinds of activities connected with the festival, including shows in restaurants, an international mass, the Folkotheque and parades during the day and evening. In addition, Radio-Canada will be giving a live broadcast of the impressive opening ceremonies.
Next week, Drummondville will be bursting with sound and colour, and I invite everyone to come and discover our own traditions and those of other countries.

Mr. Speaker, the Tory Government has betrayed elderly Canadians, and they never expected such treatment. The May 23 federal Budget attacks the well-being of elderly Canadians living on fixed incomes. It increases the cost of living for senior citizens through hidden and regressive taxes on food, drugs, and on personal tax tables which cut future purchasing power of old age benefits.
During the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Tory candidates said that they were committed to full pension reform to eliminate poverty amongst retired Canadians and to improve their standard of living. What was the reality? Through deindexing, elderly Canadians will be especially hard hit, losing almost $2 a day of disposable income by 1990.
At the present time 635,000 elderly people live below the poverty line; 450,000 are single and 80 per cent of these are women. Over the next five years the deindexing of Old Age
Security alone will add over 100,000 elderly to the poverty statistics.
The Tory Government has tried to justify the unjustifiable-the cutting of old age pensions. Hundreds of Mount Royal constituents have directed me to call upon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) today to restore full indexation of pensions now so that our senior citizens can maintain their purchasing power and have peace of mind to enjoy this summer.

Mr. Speaker, the federal Budget was not welcome news to Canadians in the tourist industry. Almost no consideration was given to the effects of budget measures such as gas increases, liquor tax increases, and other taxes on tourism.
The most recent figures show Canada continuing to fall behind in the international tourist trade. Tourism is a major job creator, but the Budget did not take this into consideration.
Now the Government has decided to remove the $30 ceiling on the domestic air transportation tax, which will take an extra $90 million a year from Canadian travellers, hurting the travel and the hospitality segments of the tourist industry.
Given that the Government has not taken one positive measure yet to assist the tourist industry, other than the signing of agreements to provide funds already budgeted, and has instead used this industry alternately as a punchbag, a doormat, and a milch-cow, the Minister should do the sensible and honest thing by resigning and recommending the dissolution of this obviously ineffective Department. It would appear that we can now hypothesize that there is a "Wilson's law"- those industries that the Government wishes to neglect, it first establishes a ministry for.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that most Members of the House are aware of the Canadian Human Rights Commission as well as its functions.
According to Chief Commissioner Fairweather, the Commission has received 31,473 inquiries, conducted 1,000 preliminary investigations, and investigated 400 cases that were jurisdictionally sound.
In addition, the Commission has an operating budget of $9 million, which some members of the NDP and the Liberal Parties in the House believe is too low. Even so, of these 400 cases that were completed, each carries a price tag of $22,500, with only a success rate of 31 per cent. With this in mind, I

June 27, 1985
feel the time has come for the Government to give the Human Rights Commission, as it functions now, a second look. Furthermore, it would seem that 400 investigations out of a population of 24.5 million would suggest that major human rights violations in Canada are very minimal.

Canada can be proud of its record on human rights and should serve as an example of tolerance to other countries.

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF NIAGARA MENNONITE SETTLEMENT
FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF NIAGARA MENNONITE SETTLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 200 years ago the first Mennonites came to Canada. The Mennonite community of Virgil-Niagara, with the assistance of Multiculturalism Canada, has published an informative historical documentary textbook commemorating the fiftieth anniversary of the first Mennonite settlement in Niagara.
The social, economic, religious, and cultural influence of the Mennonite people in Niagara is deeply woven into the fabric of the whole community, and their contributions are numerous. They have firmly established themselves in every walk of life.
Two members of the Niagara Mennonite community, Mr. Jake Froese and Mr. Bill Andres, served with distinction as Members of Parliament.
This photo-journal is a testimonial to how a people, although simple in lifestyle, yet industrious in nature and committed to strong principles, helped to build our country.
In a world in which whole races of people are persecuted for religious beliefs, oppressed, and even annihilated for the colour of their skin, the world can indeed learn a lesson from the Mennonite community's belief in peace and brotherhood. It is based on the teachings of Christ from the Sermon on the Mount, when he said: "If possible as far as it depends on you, be at peace with all men".
I am proud to be able to make this presentation of "Memoirs: 50 years of the Virgil-Niagara Mennonite Community" to the Library of the Parliament of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I asked how the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) could possibly keep a commitment that he made to my constituents and to the employees of the Chalk River Nuclear Laboratory, in particular that:
"A P.C. Government will not only maintain this facility it will consider providing additional funds to allow greater involvement".
My question asked how could the Prime Minister honour this commitment to the science community of Canada, and to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, when his Government has stated in the Budget that it will cut $100 million, or 50 per cent of the Government's research and development funding, from Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. The Prime Minister's Government has also taken $70 million of the company's earned savings which were to be used to pay for other AECL debts or accounts. Obviously, no one was answering for the Prime Minister because, for a moment, no one got up to offer a reply. We, and all Canadians, can understand why anyone would hesitate to answer for the Prime Minister's credibility on the floor of this House.
We know that this immediate cut was forced on Atomic Energy of Canada by this Government. We know that AECL asked to be left alone for two years to put its plans for additional revenue in place in order to accommodate the cuts, but nobody was listening. The Prime Minister has proven once again that his level of credibility to the nation is the lowest of any Prime Minister in Canada's history.

subtopic: SOUTH MORESBY AREA OF QUEEN CHARLOTTE ISLANDS
SOUTH MORESBY AREA OF QUEEN CHARLOTTE ISLANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for years groups of citizens around British Columbia, across Canada, and around the world have been calling on Canada to move and set aside the South Moresby area of the Queen Charlottes as an area of land and marine parks to have a true world heritage park there. It is now urgent that negotiations take place between the Council of the Haida Nations and the two levels of government to achieve this goal.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) is on the record as wishing to set this area aside from further industrial development. The Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) on June 29, 1984, as the P.C. spokesperson on environment and parks, stated:
In short, the federal Progressive Conservative Party, if in a position to do so following a federal election, would be prepared to actively participate with the B.C. Government in the establishment of a park at South Moresby.
As a member of the recently established National Committee for the Preservation of South Moresby, I join with Pierre Berton, Dr. David Suzuki, Charles Caccia, Robert Bateman, Freeman Patterson, Andy Russell, Bristol Foster, Gregg Sheehy, Farley Mowatt, and hundress of thousands of Canadians, in saying now is the time to act; the election is over.
The decision on South Moresby is expected from Victoria in the next few days. Inaction, and a lack of political vision by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Premier of British Columbia, mean, to paraphrase Jacques Cousteau: "It will be Canada's Galapagos Lost."
June 27, 1985

-on May 23 I had the honour of presenting this Government's first Budget to this House. It was a comprehensive strategy designed to end the greatest social injustice in this country, the tragic lack of meaningful jobs. It introduced measures to encourage the economic growth we need to finance social and cultural progress. It outlined a balanced and realistic plan to regain control of our spiralling debt, a compounding debt which threatens government programs in the future.
During the past month my colleagues and I have had the opportunity to discuss the budgetary strategy with many Canadians. I am pleased to report that our plan of action has been generally well received.

First, we broadened the social safety net to ensure greater fairness and to promote social justice. The second part of the strategy was to implement major reforms to the private pension system to ensure that Canadians have a fair and equal opportunity to save for their own retirement.
The third part is to put the Canada Pension Plan on a sound financial basis. 1 have commenced discussions on this subject with provincial Ministers of Finance, and we will be discussing this important issue again this fall.
The fourth and critical element is to regain control of our spiralling national debt. As I have stated on many occasions, the financial position of the Government of Canada has worsened at an accelerating rate over the past decade, particularly
Statements by Ministers
over the past two years. Previous Government decisions have created a structural budgetary imbalance which has contributed to ever-growing annual deficits and a compounding national debt.

It is important that all Canadians realize the size and urgency of our financial problem and understand why we have taken measures to deal with it in the Budget. Mr. Speaker, 1 cannot repeat this often enough.

It took 100 years for successive Canadian Governments to accumulate a debt of almost $20 billion. Less than two decades later our debt is now $200 billion and it is doubling every five years. The reason for this rapidly growing debt is simple. The Government is borrowing additional funds each year to cover the interest charges on past debt.
Let us look at these figures carefully. In the early 1970s our annual interest payments on the debt were about $2 billion. In the late 1970s those interest charges had risen to $8 billion. This year they will total $26 billion, and if we fail to change our ways, interest charges at the end of this decade could approach $50 billion per year. Some Canadians have asked what harm deficits do to them. Well, there is harm. The growing interest charges to finance those deficits are crowding out worth-while programs, programs which benefit many of us. We have to take control of our debt or those interest payments will simply overwhelm us.
There is another aspect which directly affects our senior citizens. Over the past 15 years, high inflation caused by rising deficits and mounting debt literally wiped out the savings of our sernior citizens. That was a time when there was real cause for concern among our seniors.

This means only one thing, that all Canadians will be affected, rich and poor alike. The Minister knows that that has a negative effect on the economy in terms of our competitive position. It also puts a regressive additional burden on everyone.
Since the Minister addressed the issue of alternative sources of funding, and since we will be dealing with Budget Bills when we return in the fall, we are hoping that this is not the only change of mind experienced by the Government on its Budget. We are pleased that the Government has changed its mind on this issue, but we will fight hard to get the Government to change its position on other unfair aspects of the Budget.
It was interesting to hear the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) talk about all the regressivity and tax unfairness in the Budget, as if it were not the Liberal Party which reduced taxes on the rich in 1982 by almost $2 billion. The Liberals are always good social democrats when they are in opposition, but they are Conservatives when they are in power. That is the problem with the Liberal Party of Canada.

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: A pox on both their sides.

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
We will see about that. When we get around to debating the Budget Bills, we will have to look at alternative proposals. In terms of the part-time surtax on
June 27, 1985

incomes over $40,000 per year, people can avoid it because it is on federal taxable income. If they use the loopholes, as the Prime Minister knows well, they could end up not even paying it. I say rhetorically to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and to the Prime Minister: Why not restore taxation levels to upper income Canadians, the marginal tax rates, to what they were before the Liberals cut them in 1982? That would give them $1.7 billion, year in and year out, to redistribute downward to the poor people of Canada.
There were good aspects of the Western Accord on energy. We in this Party were pleased to see the producing provinces, particularly Alberta and Saskatchewan, obtain a larger share of the revenue. However, we saw no economic sense or economic justice in providing some $400 million to $500 million in additional revenue to multinational oil companies for oil which they had already discovered.

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: And they want more.

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
They want more, that is correct. If the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister are looking for additional sources of revenue, why impose a one-cent per litre tax on gasoline at the pumps which affects ordinary Canadians? Why do they not go after the multinational oil companies and get them to pay their fair share of taxes?
I want to conclude with two points. The first one concerns a very important question. The principle of universality was at stake in this issue. If we had gone the route of the Budget, and if we had followed the thinking of the vast majority of members of the Conservative Party, as I understood it and as it was expressed in the debate, we would have established a two-class system for pensioners, and a few years down the road the basic pension would have had marginal significance for the people of Canada. We on this side of the House are pleased, not simply with a political victory, although I think it was a political victory, but for the sake of the history of our country. For the last 30 years, we have been gradually building up- and we thought it was an accepted notion in the minds of members of all Parties-a social security system in this land of ours which says that everything is not a market-place commodity. When it comes to medical services, education and pensions, it does not matter if one is a doctor, a lawyer, a logger, a banker or a very poor person; eveyone is entitled to a basic program of that kind.
In conclusion, the Government backed down, not because of a newly perceived sense of fairness, but because there was opposition to a perceived unfairness in the Budget. I pay particular tribute to the older people of the country, from Halifax and St. John's in the east to Victoria in the west, who were not the passive creatures about whom some people like to write in modern society. They were men and women who perceived that the Government was going in the wrong direction and got their message through. We on this side of the House did our job. There is no doubt about that. It shows what can be done in a parliamentary system, even when the Government has a large majority.

I conclude by expressing my appreciation to the pensioners of Canada for fighting their cause, for fighting a just cause and winning.

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) has dealt with the issue of fairness, but I wanted to direct a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) with respect to the fundamental economic asssumptions upon which the Budget proceeds, especially with respect to the sales tax that will be imposed in some respects on July 1, and of course the additional gasoline tax about which we learned today.
Specifically, as the Minister knows, the Economic Council of Canada conducted simulation studies about two years ago which showed that a reduction in sales tax would decrease the rate of inflation, would increase consumer demand and would increase jobs. I think the Minister of Finance would agree that in the long term his deficit problem has to be resolved by growth, not through cuts in taxes. Next year alone he shows only a $1 billion reduction in the deficit. Has the Minister conducted simulation studies, not on the effect of increasing taxes, but on the effect of decreasing taxes? If he has done so, could he table them in the House so that we could compare them with the scenario presented to us in the Budget?

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always amused by these probing questions from the Liberal Party, the Party which says that it would control the deficit. When we look back and see what happened over the past 10 or 15 years, starting from the time when the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) held my portfolio, we know that all these questions are a lot of hot air. They do not have any idea what they would do. The Leader of the Opposition said that he would have cut the deficit by $15 billion if he had remained in the job of Prime Minister. I ask him and I ask the Financial critic of the Liberal Party: If they do not like the way in which we propose to cut the deficit, let us hear what they have to say. We will have four months of consultation in the fall of this year, leading up to the next Budget. I would be delighted to hear what they have to say about how we can get on top of the deficit problem.
When the Leader of the Opposition was Minister of Finance, the spending of the Government rose 30 per cent in one year, and he says in a righteous way: "Show me the impact of what you have just done".
The impact of what I have just done is that we will maintain control of the fiscal problem, so that we will not have the runway deficits which we have experienced over the past four years, where deficits went from $14 billion, to $23 billion, to $30 billion, to $35 billion. That is what we have to stop. The sooner the Hon. Member gets that through his thick skull, the better this country will be.

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intended to pose my question in a serious way and tried to be helpful to the Minister of Finance. We recognize his dilemma and we recognize the

June 27, 1985
Statements by Ministers
dilemma faced in this Budget document when he shows us that, with all this pain and suffering, the deficit between 1985-86 and 1986-87 comes down by $1 billion, from $33.7 billion to $32.7 billion. Magically, by 1990-91, he tells us, it will be down by $20 billion. Would the Minister show us the calculations for those intervening years, which we have not received and which were not included in the Budget documents? That is one point.
My other question is in direct response to his question when he asked what we would do. Elas he considered the opposite scenario? If he has, can we see the simulation? He told us on March 1 that increased taxes would dampen demand and that there was room on the expenditure side. His seat-mate, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen), is chairing the committee looking at the expenditure side. We have not seen results of any concrete nature from that exercise. I say to the Minister of Finance: Let us look at this documentation in the course of the debate to see if there is a better way to go, because we believe that there is. This is not an expansionary Budget and expansion is required if this country is going to pull out of its deficit. It is not going to come about, I suggest to the Minister, by these kinds of taxes and these modest cuts that he has come forward with.

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have heard this argument before: Let us hope for growth and growth will solve all our problems. Let me remind the Hon. Member that last year in the United States I think they had growth of 6.9 per cent, and what happened? The deficit went down $15 billion. In Canada we had growth of 5 per cent, a pretty good growth rate. What happened to the deficit in the country? It went up about $6 billion. This is the sort of thing that shows there is a little bit of hokum in the argument that the Hon. Member puts out on the floor of the House of Commons.
Let me just put the numbers back to him. We are spending this year $26 billion on interest costs; we are spending $9.4 billion on defence; $2.1 billion on overseas aid. Which of those does he think he can cut? We have major statutory programs, unemployment insurance, family allowance, benefits for the elderly, EPF, the Canada Assistance Program. We have $31.6 billion in all the programs of Government, apart from those. That is why we have to be looking at some other ways, as we have outlined in this Budget, to come to terms with the deficit problem.
I will go back to what the Leader of the NDP-probably he is more the Leader of the Opposition than the current one is- said, that we will have our social programs and then we will borrow money to pay for them. If we borrow $1,000 to pay for part of a social program, in seven years' time in today's earnings that will be $1,000 that we will have paid in interest costs and we will still not have paid the money back. That is the problem that we have to get over. I think the Hon. Member knows it but either he is not admitting it or what he is saying is, "I don't know how to solve the problem and I am very happy that I am in the Opposition". I say to him, we are
very happy he is too and all Canadians are happy because we cannot have any more of the type of runaway spending that we have had over the past 15 or 20 years.

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

He also said as recently as March 1 that there was room on the expenditure side.
Is he telling us today and did he tell us in the Budget, perhaps based on the advise that he received from his seat-mate, that he could find no room on the expenditure side and that he has decided that, notwithstanding the dampening effect of taxes, that is the way to get at the deficit? If that is the way to get at the deficit, how does he explain how the deficit is to be reduced by $20 billion by the year 1991 when it will only come down $1 billion, by his own numbers, by the year 1987?

Mr. Speaker, let me ask the Hon. Member to go back and read the Budget again, if he ever did read it. Seventy-five billion dollars is going to be reduced from the accumulated debt between now and 1990-91. That is in the Budget papers. Eighty per cent of that is on spending cuts. Only 15 per cent is going to be found through tax increases.
We have gone through all Departments of Government. My colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), as the Hon. Member points out, is the chairman of the task force looking at programs, and there will be more spending cuts, more efficiencies and less waste as we go through the process of this task force.
I remind him that 80 per cent of what we will be doing over the next five or six years will be found on the expenditure side. That demonstrates the amount of waste, the amount of inefficiencies, the lack of attention that the previous Government allowed to go on. If we could find that amount of money, surely they could have done a slightly better job when they were in power. That is the sort of difference we are facing here with this Government in power and not the previous Government.

Mr. Speaker, I have three questions that I would like to put to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). The Minister of Finance will be aware, as my Leader has pointed out, that one of the reasons, perhaps one of the major reasons why we have an increasing deficit today is that personal sales tax and corporate tax simply are not flowing in to Government as we had expected and experienced in the past, as a result of the economic downturn and the economic malaise. He will also know that it is sound business practice that to make money one has to invest money. In other words, to gather sales tax and corporate and personal income tax one has to invest to see that that happens. Would it not make sense in terms of deficit
June 27, 1985

reduction for the Minister of Finance to take steps to encourage economic development in a direct way? I will use two examples. The mayors of Canada indicated that there are $14 billion of necessary municipal works that must be conducted in the country. Can the Minister of Finance think of a better time to get those kinds of projects under way? Reforestation projects are needed in virtually every province in the country, much more than the rather small step that was taken as a result of some of the ERDA agreements that were recently signed.
I would like him to comment on that. In other words, if he is serious about economic development, why not take some stimulative steps to ensure that it takes place?
Second I want to ask the Minister of Finance what he thinks about the proposal put forward by my Leader in terms of deficit reduction when he said, why not return to the tax levels of 1982 that were changed in the MacEachen Liberal Budget. That would result today in an inflow of taxes of about $1.7 billion per year. Again, this is just a practical example. The Minister has indicated he wants to hear some specifics.
Third, I want to ask the Minister of Finance if he has confidence in his Budget, in his economic statement and the economic policies therein. When I asked him in the last two or three weeks to provide me, through the Access to Information Act, with the impact studies flowing from the Budget in terms of its impact on unemployment, on regional economic development and similar kinds of impacts, the Minister of Finance signed a letter to me saying that that information would not be available. If the Minister has confidence, why not provide that material? If the Minister has faith in what he is doing, why would he not share this? What is he trying to hide?

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

Member's attention to the last paragraph of my remarks in which I said that elderly Canadians can only feel secure if we have a financially responsible Government and a healthy, growing economy. maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:

Member goes back and compares the tax regime before the NEP and now, he will see that the oil companies in Canada are not as well off. I have never heard the Hon. Member acknowledge that. I have never heard him congratulate either myself or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) for doing this.
What we have tried to do is to provide a taxation regime for the oil industry which is comparable to tax regimes in other industries. The Hon. Member knows what happened in the industry because he and I were both energy critics at the same time. He knows what happened to the oil and gas industry in western Canada. He knows about the companies which were shut, the stores which were boarded up and the motels which went out of business because people were not travelling through the foothills of Alberta. What we are trying to do is to remove a discrimination which was hurting an industry in Alberta and also other parts of Canada where there are major suppliers to the oil and gas industry.
One cannot have it both ways on this whole question of taxation or economics. If we want to have jobs created, we have to provide the taxation regime and the economic environment to encourage people to go out and invest money in new projects and create jobs. If we take that away, if we remove that environment and develop a tax system in such a way that
it takes away from those companies, those jobs are not going to be created. Either the Hon. Member wants to put people out of jobs or he goes along with it.
Since September 4, 271,000 jobs have been created, so something must be going right. Something must be going right in this country if we are able to see that sort of performance here. That is what we want to try to reinforce.

The cost of excavating the soil and re-landscaping the affected properties is estimated at $552,000. The cost of storing the soils (an estimated $400,000), as is contemplated in an agreement between Canada and Ontario, will be borne by the province.
2.	The possibility of the houses being bought by either the provincial or federal Government has been analysed. To buy the 39 properties directly affected would cost approximately $2.7 million. However, this action would likely not satisfy the concerns of owners of neighbouring properties which are not contaminated. A number of these owners are involved in litigation, claiming substantial damages, together with owners of directly affected properties. To buy all 104 houses on McClure Crescent and an additional four backing on to the Crescent would cost approximately $8.1 million. Even then, there may be some who feel the line has been drawn too closely. To purchase all houses within a zone equivalent to the uninhabited area around the temporary storage site for the soil proposed by the Province of Ontario would involve an expenditure of tens of millions of dollars.
3.	(a) and (b) There have been two legal actions relating to proposed relocation of the soil. The first was an action by the Townships of Essa and Tosoronto to prevent relocation of the soil to Canadian Forces Base, Borden in 1981. The legal costs incurred by the Atomic Energy Control Board, which was the proponent of that move, were $5,000. In addition, an estimated $2,000 of an AECB official's time was involved in defending the action.
There is currently an injunction action before the Federal Court, in which Waste Not Wanted Inc. is seeking to prevent Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. and the federal Government from relocating the soil to a storage site provided by the Province of Ontario in a sparsely populated area of Scarborough under an agreement with the federal Government.
Expenses incurred by AECL and the Government in defending this action are approximately $250,000, in addition to the time of the AECL, EM&R and Department of Justice staff involved in defending the action.
